query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers, sustained loading induces progressive plastic (creep) deformation primarily through the combined effects of interface-mediated dislocation pile-ups and strain‐induced modulation of short-range order (MSRO). Varying the nanoscale layer thickness and compositional gradients will systematically alter the local lattice distortion near interfaces, thereby tuning the balance between dislocation accumulation and MSRO evolution and, hence, the overall creep rate.
generation.material_initial_state: FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers with nanoscale coatings that inherently possess compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and pre-existing or predisposed short-range order.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the nanoscale layer thickness and compositional modulation across the multilayer structure.
generation.conditions: Subject samples to sustained mechanical creep loading (e.g., at an elevated temperature or under prolonged room-temperature stress) that promotes time-dependent deformation while maintaining the nanoscale multilayer architecture.
generation.structural_mediator: The multilayer interfaces, which restrict dislocation nucleation and motion, thereby localizing strain and influencing the evolution of MSRO in adjacent regions.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained load, the multilayer interfaces impede dislocation motion, leading to localized strain accumulation that triggers or modifies the formation of MSRO. This evolving MSRO, in turn, alters local lattice resistance—either enhancing hardening by stabilizing dislocation obstacles or promoting softening when disrupted—thus governing the effective creep rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with thicker layers (or with compositional gradients that reduce the stabilizing effect of MSRO) will exhibit enhanced dislocation pile-ups and a higher creep rate, whereas samples engineered to promote robust MSRO at the interfaces will show reduced dislocation mobility and a lower creep rate compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Multilayer specimens with uniform nanoscale coatings and homogeneous composition under the same sustained loading conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies as long as the nanoscale multilayer structure is preserved and testing conditions do not induce other dominant deformation mechanisms (such as phase transformations or diffusion-dominated creep).
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of dislocation pile-up versus MSRO evolution in determining the creep rate remain uncertain; subtle variations in temperature or stress may shift the dominant mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multilayer samples: (1) a baseline set with uniform nanoscale layers and consistent composition, and (2) an experimental set with systematically varied layer thickness and controlled compositional gradients. Subject both sets to identical sustained creep loading conditions. Employ in situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and diffraction techniques to observe dislocation structures and MSRO evolution in the vicinity of the interfaces while concurrently measuring creep strain over time.
measurements: Creep strain versus time curves to extract creep rates
High-resolution microscopy to quantify dislocation density and pile-up structures at the multilayer interfaces
Local structural and chemical analysis (e.g., via STEM or diffraction) to assess the formation and evolution of MSRO
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental group's variations in layer thickness and composition do not lead to significant or systematic differences in the measured creep rates, dislocation pile-up patterns, and MSRO evolution compared to the baseline group, then the hypothesis—that interface-mediated dislocation barriers and MSRO modulation govern creep deformation—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: When the loading rate increases to 2.5 mN/s, the creep stress exponent n for the alloy with x = 0.5 abruptly shifts to 1.15, as illustrated in Figure 10b. This change indicates that under these conditions, the alloy’s creep mechanism transitions to diffusion creep. At this point, the alloy’s dislocation activation volume V* is 0.21 b3 (Figure 11), which is typically associated with the non-uniform nucleation of dislocations, and creep deformation occurs through direct atom–vacancy exchange []. These findings suggest that the creep deformation mechanism of the same alloy can vary under different loading rates. At high loading rates, the alloy may exhibit creep behavior distinct from that observed at lower rates.

Chemical short-range order in disordered solid solutions often emerges with specific heat treatments. Unlike thermally activated ordering, mechanically derived short-range order (MSRO) in a multi-principal-element Fe40Mn40Cr10Co10 (at%) alloy originates from tensile deformation at 77 K, and its degree/extent can be tailored by adjusting the loading rates under quasistatic conditions. The mechanical response and multi-length-scale characterisation pointed to the minor contribution of MSRO formation to yield strength, mechanical twinning, and deformation-induced displacive transformation. Scanning and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and the anlaysis of electron diffraction patterns revealed the microstructural features responsible for MSRO and the dependence of the ordering degree/extent on the applied strain rates. Here, we show that underpinned by molecular dynamics, MSRO in the alloys with low stacking-fault energies forms when loaded at 77 K, and these systems that offer different perspectives on the process of strain-induced ordering transition are driven by crystalline lattice defects (dislocations and stacking faults). decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy alloys first identified that the conventional mechanisms (e.g. dislocation slip in ordered lattices) do not fully capture the role of compositional complexity and lattice distortion. Initial work (PMC4949441) demonstrated that dislocation motion in HEAs can be markedly different—featuring undissociated superdislocations—while subsequent atomistic simulations (PMC4976365) highlighted the effect of chemical clustering and short‐range ordering under high-strain deformation. More recent work (PMC9646780 and PMC12898549) has revealed that mechanically induced short-range order and nanoscale elastic inhomogeneities (undulations) emerge under applied stress, suggesting that local strain fields and interface effects can alter dislocation nucleation and mobility. In parallel, conventional metallic multilayer studies have typically been used to balance strength and ductility but do not account for the subtle interlayer interactions of HEA systems. In all, researchers have sequentially moved from identifying dislocation-based mechanisms in homogeneous HEAs to uncovering strain‐induced ordering and nanoscale elastic responses, yet these investigations have largely ignored the complication of a multilayer geometry.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings under sustained loading which mechanistic pathway dominates: whether creep and progressive plastic deformation result primarily from dislocation interactions impaired by multilayer interfaces or from an evolving, strain-induced short-range order that modulates local lattice softening or hardening. In other words, the interplay between interface-driven dislocation pile-ups and MSRO evolution, especially under nanoscale confinement, has not been decisively isolated or measured under the creep regime.
decision.lever: Systematic variation of nanoscale layer thickness and controlled compositional modulation across the multilayers to tune interface spacing and local lattice distortion, while performing sustained loading (creep) tests
decision.why: Because previous studies have established that dislocation behavior and strain-induced short-range order significantly affect deformation in bulk and single-phase HEAs, the next logical step is a controlled experiment in multilayers. By varying layer thickness and composition, one can isolate the relative contributions of interface-mediated dislocation interactions versus local MSRO evolution. Observations such as layer-thickness‐dependent creep rate changes and evidence of localized ordering (via in situ or advanced characterization) would support the hypothesis, while failure to detect systematic variations under controlled changes would falsify it.
